newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU summit inches towards agreement on EMU, treaty.
newsitem.headline: EU summit inches towards agreement on EMU, treaty.

text.p: European Union leaders edged towards agreement on a strategy to promote growth and jobs on Monday, raising prospects of keeping their troubled drive for a single currency on track, diplomats said.

While their finance ministers met separately, the 15 leaders ploughed through the painstaking business of putting finishing touches to a new EU treaty, designed to pave the way for the 15-member bloc's enlargement and signal a Citizens' Europe.

In their first success, they agreed on the content of an employment chapter to be added to a revised Maastricht treaty on European union, allowing for limited, EU-backed incentives and pilot projects and annual guidelines to member states on measures to promote job-creation.

With financial markets calm but waiting to pounce on any sign of problems, ministers made resolutely upbeat comments on their way into the talks about prospects of meeting the new Socialist French government's demands for a resolution on employment to go alongside a pact limiting budget deficits.

"There will be an agreement today and a text by this evening," said Dutch Finance Minister Gerrit Zalm, who had reported substantial progress after a finance ministers' late night working dinner on Sunday.

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, true to his country's reputation as Europe's stickler for fiscal discipline, reaffirmed as he entered Monday's meeting there would be "no more money" for job-creation schemes.

Diplomats said ministers were looking to two previously untapped sources of existing funds to promote job-creating schemes -- the one billion European currency units profit of the European Investment Bank and roughly another one billion ECUs in the "war chest" of the European Coal and Steel Community.

Conservative French President Jacques Chirac, with Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin sitting at his side, appealed to summit leaders to try to give Europe a more social face and do more for the bloc's 18 million unemployed.

"We must reconcile European citizens with Europe. That means setting clearly priorities. It also means giving the Union more effective ways of supporting member states' efforts and ensuring the preservation and reinforcement of the Euorpean social model," Chirac said, according to a text of his remarks.

Diplomats said the leaders were trying hard not to let the tug-of-war between France and Germany over how to proceed with monetary union disrupt their negotiations of a new EU treaty, due to be completed by Tuesday night.
"They are trying to do it in parallel, but (the row) also affects the mood," one said.
Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok admitted that the summit was effectively two-pronged -- agreeing the stability pact and finalising an inter-governmental conference treaty review.
"We go for a double result. We want to have a good result on the treaty and, on top of that, we hope to have an agreement on the stability pact," he told reporters.

An official close to Jospin said he expected an agreement on a document including both the stability pact limiting the budget deficits of members of the single currency to three percent of gross domestic product, and the growth and employment resolution, by early on Monday afternoon.
However, the damaging rift between Paris and Bonn has laid bare the two core EU members' fundamental differences over how to cement monetary union, due to be launched in January 1999.
"In Germany there is a real distrust of everything political," Luxembourg Premier Jean-Claude Juncker said in an interview in Le Figaro. "In France there is a real distrust of everything economic."

EU leaders will also consider whether to hold a special "jobs summit" in Luxembourg in October, where they could focus more directly on France's desire to put employment at the top of the agenda, diplomats said.
